newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African money market shortage, short rates climb.
newsitem.headline: S.African money market shortage, short rates climb.

text.p: Lack of expected government spending flows pushed the South African money market shortage up around 600 million rand on Wednesday, in turn putting pressure on short-term interest rates, traders said.
The Reserve Bank indicated the shortage higher at 9.697 billion rand on Tuesday from 9.064 billion rand on Monday.

Commercial banks quoted three-month NCD rates higher on the news at between 17.10 and 17.30 percent bid from 17.10 and 17.20 percent bid before. The 90-day BA rate was left unchanged at between 16.30 to 16.60 percent.

"Government spending was expected to filter through to the market on Wednesday and that failure (of the expected flows) has put some pressure on the shortage," a senior dealer said, adding that flows should still come in over the next couple of days.

Referring to talk earlier this week that the Reserve Bank could facilitate access to liquid assets, he said some banks had spoken to the central bank about taking in longer-dated bonds and switching them for liquids but no confirmation had been received on the matter.

Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals had said the central bank was considering helping banks gain access to liquid assets held by government's pension fund investment manager, following appeals from leading banks for help to avert a prime rate hike.

Commercial banks' margins have came under increasing pressure over the last few weeks following renewed weakness in the rand and investment outflows which has resulted in a cash crunch in the money market.
"It looks as if this market will have to sit tight and that's exactly what it's doing," another senior trader said.
Banks wanted to see a higher prime overdraft rate but the solution ultimately was more money in the system or a drop in credit demand.

"We need serious cash inflow into this country to alleviate the shortage...once the shortage is down we won't have this bun fight for rates and if that is coupled with an easing in credit we will obviously have a lot more liquidity, interest rates could come down and all other fundamentals would start looking better again," he said.
The wild card remained the ongoing volatility in the currency market, other traders said.
"It's a hell of a guessing game at the moment," one said.

Traders said there was speculation that some of the "big four" commercial banks had borrowed foreign exchange offshore to ease the liquidity squeeze but they would not drawn on how much might have been borrowed.
Bank rate currently stands at 16 percent while the prime lending rate of banks is 19.25 percent.
